title: Academic References and Further Reading
text:
The lectures in this course introduce each concept conceptually: enough mechanism to configure, use, and debug it, without the full architectural detail. This page maps every simplified concept to the authoritative document where the complete story lives, so that a curious student — or a future project — can go one level deeper with a known-good source instead of a random blog.
Each lecture gets its own section. Entries are added as lectures are revised.

title: Academic References and Further Reading
text:
If a link stops working
Links below point at the current official locations (verified 2026-07-17). If one rots:

ST documents (RM…, PM…, UM…, MB… numbers): search the document number at st.com; the number uniquely identifies the document and survives site reorganizations.
Arm documents (DDI… numbers): search at developer.arm.com.
Books: available through the university library or the cited publisher; Lee & Seshia is free and legal at leeseshia.org.

title: Academic References and Further Reading
section: Primary documents used throughout the course
text:
Primary documents used throughout the course



Short name
Full citation
What it is for




RM0368
STMicroelectronics, RM0368: STM32F401xB/C and STM32F401xD/E advanced Arm®-based 32-bit MCUs — Reference Manual (PDF)
The register-level truth for every peripheral on our chip: GPIO, SYSCFG, EXTI, timers, ADC, I2C, SPI, DMA


PM0214
STMicroelectronics, PM0214: STM32 Cortex®-M4 MCUs and MPUs programming manual (PDF)
The processor core seen from software: instruction set, exception model, NVIC, SysTick, core registers


UM1724
STMicroelectronics, UM1724: STM32 Nucleo-64 boards (MB1136) — User Manual (PDF)
The board itself: B1 and LD2 circuits, jumpers, ST-LINK, power, board revision differences


MB1136 schematic
STMicroelectronics, MB1136 schematic pack, rev C-04 (PDF)
The actual circuit diagram of the Nucleo-F401RE — the version used in lecture


UM1725
STMicroelectronics, UM1725: Description of STM32F4 HAL and low-layer drivers (PDF)
Signature and behavior of every HAL_… function the labs use


Yiu 2014
J. Yiu, The Definitive Guide to ARM® Cortex®-M3 and Cortex®-M4 Processors, 3rd ed., Newnes, 2014. ISBN 978-0-12-408082-9
The standard book-length treatment of the core: pipeline, exceptions, NVIC, low-power, debug


DDI 0403
Arm Ltd., ARMv7-M Architecture Reference Manual (Arm DDI 0403)
The formal architecture specification — for when even Yiu is not precise enough


Lee & Seshia
E. A. Lee and S. A. Seshia, Introduction to Embedded Systems: A Cyber-Physical Systems Approach, 2nd ed., MIT Press, 2017 — free PDF
The academic textbook view: interrupts, concurrency, real-time reasoning


White 2024
E. White, Making Embedded Systems, 2nd ed., O’Reilly, 2024
Practical engineering judgment: interrupt hygiene, debouncing, system design patterns


C11
ISO/IEC 9899:2011, Programming languages — C (link is N1570, the final public draft, PDF)
The C language standard; final authority on volatile, integer types, undefined behavior

section: L04 — Pointers, Structures, Bits, Registers, and GPIO
text:
L04 — Pointers, Structures, Bits, Registers, and GPIO
The lecture builds GPIOA->BSRR = (1U << 5); from its parts: addresses, pointers, structures, masks, and the GPIO registers.



Concept as taught
Where the full story is




Addresses and memory — “memory is a numbered collection of storage locations”
PM0214 Rev 10, §2.2 Memory model — p. 28: the real Cortex-M4 memory map, including where peripherals live


Pointers: & and *
C11 (N1570), §6.5.3.2 Address and indirection operators — p. 106


Structures and . / ->
C11 (N1570), §6.7.2.1 Structure and union specifiers — p. 130


Bitwise operators, masks, the U suffix
C11 (N1570), §6.5.7 Bitwise shift operators — p. 112, then §6.5.10–6.5.12 for &, ^, |; §6.5.7 also explains why shifting signed values can be undefined behavior — the reason the U suffix matters


CMSIS register names — “the device header supplies the definition”
The actual stm32f401xe.h device header (GPIO_TypeDef, GPIOA_BASE); Yiu 2014, ch. 2 on what CMSIS standardizes


volatile register members
C11 (N1570), §6.7.3 — p. 140; M. Barr, How to Use C’s volatile Keyword


Peripheral clock gating — “enable the clock first”
RM0368 Rev 6, RCC_AHB1ENR — p. 118; the RCC chapter (§6) explains why clocks are gated: power


GPIO block, MODER, BSRR
RM0368 Rev 6, §8 GPIO — p. 146; registers: GPIOx_MODER — p. 158, GPIOx_BSRR — p. 161 — including what the lecture skips: OTYPER, OSPEEDR, PUPDR

title: Academic References and Further Reading
text:
L05 — GPIO and Hardware Abstraction
The lecture connects every HAL name to the register behavior taught in L04: same hardware, second interface.



Concept as taught
Where the full story is




The HAL GPIO API — GPIO_InitTypeDef, HAL_GPIO_Init, WritePin / TogglePin / ReadPin
UM1725 Rev 8, GPIO functions — p. 447


What the HAL actually executes
The source of stm32f4xx_hal_gpio.c — HAL_GPIO_WritePin is a single BSRR write


HAL names → register bits — GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT_PP, GPIO_NOPULL, speed
RM0368 Rev 6, §8 GPIO — p. 146; registers: GPIOx_MODER — p. 158, GPIOx_PUPDR — p. 159, GPIOx_BSRR — p. 161


Floating inputs, pull-up / pull-down
RM0368 §8.3 (I/O port control); the electronics context in any circuits text — the lecture’s claim is only that an undriven CMOS input is undefined


B1 circuit — external pull-up, active-low
MB1136 schematic rev C-04; UM1724 Rev 17, push-buttons — p. 24; confirmed against the ST Nucleo BSP source


Why abstraction layers exist — and what they cost
White 2024, ch. 2 (creating system diagrams / layering); Yiu 2014, ch. 2 (what CMSIS standardizes and why)


Polling and its limits — “the loop asks again and again”
Forward pointer: the L06 row Polling vs. interrupts above

title: Academic References and Further Reading
text:
L06 — GPIO Interrupts
The lecture walks one button press through five plain-language stages (PRESS → NOTICE → ASK → LOOK UP → RUN YOUR CODE). Each simplification below names the document that removes it.
Page-anchored links (#page=N) below open the PDF at the cited page in the browser viewer. Page numbers were verified against the document revisions named in each entry (2026-07-17); if ST publishes a new revision, the section numbers in the text remain the reliable pointer.



Concept as taught
Where the full story is




Polling vs. interrupts — “polling asks again and again”
Lee & Seshia, ch. 10 Input and Output (interrupt mechanisms, latency, and when polling is actually the better design); Yiu 2014, §4.5


What really happens between ASK and RUN YOUR CODE — register stacking, vector fetch, exception entry/return (we skipped this entirely)
PM0214 Rev 10, §2.3 Exception model — p. 37; Yiu 2014, ch. 8 (including the 12-cycle entry sequence and tail-chaining); DDI 0403, §B1.5 for the formal definition


EXTI — “a set of hardware edge detectors”
RM0368 Rev 6, §10 EXTI — p. 205: block diagram, IMR/EMR/RTSR/FTSR/SWIER/PR registers, the event-vs-interrupt distinction we did not cover


SYSCFG routing — “a four-bit field selects the port”
RM0368 Rev 6, SYSCFG_EXTICR4 — p. 143


Pending bit and write-1-to-clear
RM0368 Rev 6, EXTI_PR — p. 211; the same rc_w1 convention appears in many STM32 peripherals


NVIC — “enable, priority, deliver”
PM0214 Rev 10, §4.2 NVIC — p. 208; Yiu 2014, ch. 7 — including what we postponed: priority levels, preemption, sub-priority, nesting


Vector table and the startup file
PM0214 Rev 10, §2.3.4 Vector table — p. 40; Yiu 2014, §4.4 and §8.5; the generated startup_stm32f401retx.s in every CubeMX-generated project is the concrete instance


EXTI15_10_IRQHandler / HAL helper / callback chain
UM1725 Rev 8, GPIO functions — p. 447 (HAL_GPIO_EXTI_IRQHandler, HAL_GPIO_EXTI_Callback); the ~10-line source of the helper in stm32f4xx_hal_gpio.c is worth reading in the lab


volatile — “read the stored value each time”
C11 (N1570), §6.7.3 — p. 140; M. Barr, How to Use C’s volatile Keyword, Barr Group. Note what the lecture only hints at: volatile does not make read-modify-write atomic — see Lee & Seshia, ch. 11 on shared-variable concurrency


ISR ↔︎ main() shared-variable pattern (button_event)
Lee & Seshia, ch. 11 (race conditions, atomicity); White 2024, interrupt chapter (keep-ISRs-short discipline and its reasons)


Switch bounce and the 80 ms guard
J. Ganssle, A Guide to Debouncing, 2nd ed., The Ganssle Group, 2008: measured bounce data for real switches (the “settles within ~10 ms” claim comes from here), plus hardware and software debounce alternatives


B1 circuit — external pull-up, active-low
MB1136 schematic rev C-04; UM1724 Rev 17, push-buttons — p. 24 — check the board revision: later MB1136 revisions changed the B1 circuit, which affects the pull configuration the lab assumes

title: Academic References and Further Reading
text:
L07 — Timers
The lecture builds one mental model — clock → PSC → CNT → ARR → update event — and consumes it by polling, by interrupt, and as a 1 ms tick.



Concept as taught
Where the full story is




The time base — prescaler, counter, auto-reload, update event
RM0368 Rev 6, §13 TIM2 to TIM5 — p. 316; registers (§13.4 — p. 353)


Where the 16 MHz comes from — clock tree, APB timer-clock ×2 rule
RM0368 Rev 6, §6.2 Clocks — p. 94


HAL TIM base API — handle, Base_Init, Base_Start_IT, callback
UM1725 Rev 8, TIM functions — p. 1065


The interrupt path — reused from L06
The L06 rows above; the only new element is the request name TIM2_IRQn


Tick-based scheduling and why blocking delays hurt
Lee & Seshia, ch. 10–11; White 2024, timer and main-loop chapters


SysTick — the Cortex-M core timer behind HAL_Delay (not covered)
PM0214 Rev 10, §4.5 SysTick timer — p. 246

title: Academic References and Further Reading
text:
L08 — Pulse-Width Modulation
The lecture adds the capture/compare channel to L07’s time base and uses it in the compare direction: ARR owns the frequency, CCR owns the duty.



Concept as taught
Where the full story is




PWM mode — pin high while CNT < CCR
RM0368 Rev 6, §13.3.9 PWM mode — p. 336, including what the lecture skips: center-aligned mode, PWM mode 2


Channel registers
TIMx_CCMR1 — p. 362, TIMx_CCER — p. 366, TIMx_CCR1 — p. 367


Handing the pin to the timer — alternate function
RM0368 Rev 6, GPIOx_AFRL — p. 162; the pin-to-AF table is the STM32F401RE datasheet (DS10086), Alternate function mapping — search the DS number at st.com


HAL PWM API
UM1725 Rev 8, TIM functions — p. 1065


The servo pulse contract — 50 Hz frame, 1–2 ms pulse
Hobby-servo convention, not an ST document: any RC-servo datasheet (e.g., SG90, S3003) states the same 20 ms / 1–2 ms numbers


Why the average works — PWM into slow loads
White 2024, output/actuator chapters; the RC-filter demo linked from the deck shows it interactively

title: Academic References and Further Reading
text:
L09 — Input Capture
The same channel, reversed: an edge on the pin captures the free-running counter into CCR — a hardware timestamp.



Concept as taught
Where the full story is




Input capture — edge copies CNT into CCR
RM0368 Rev 6, §13.3.5 Input capture mode — p. 333


Automated duty measurement
RM0368 Rev 6, §13.3.6 PWM input mode — p. 334 — the hardware version of the paired-channel trick, at the cost of the whole timer


Direct vs indirect inputs, the filter, overcapture
TIMx_CCMR1 — p. 362 (CCxS, ICF), TIMx_CCER — p. 366; overcapture flags in the TIMx_SR description


HAL capture API
UM1725 Rev 8, TIM functions — p. 1065; HAL_TIM_ReadCapturedValue — p. 1097


Ultrasonic ranging — echo width → distance
HC-SR04 datasheet (community-published; no ST equivalent): 10 µs trigger, echo width, the /58 cm constant

title: Academic References and Further Reading
text:
L10 — Analog-to-Digital Conversion
The lecture builds counts↔︎volts fluency on one convention (mV = raw × 3300 / 4095), one clock (PCLK2 ÷ 2 = 8 MHz), and one converter (the SAR core).



Concept as taught
Where the full story is




The ADC itself — 12-bit SAR, one converter on the F401
RM0368 Rev 6, §11 ADC — p. 213


The ADC clock — PCLK2 ÷ 2 = 8 MHz, 36 MHz ceiling
§11.3.2 ADC clock — p. 215


Channels — 16 external doors + the internal sensors
§11.3.3 Channel selection — p. 215; §11.9 Temperature sensor — p. 226


Single vs continuous conversion
§11.3.4–11.3.5 — p. 216; what the lecture skips: injected channels, the analog watchdog, external triggers (§11.6 — p. 222)


Sampling time and source impedance
§11.5 Channel-wise programmable sampling time — p. 222; the hard electrical limits (max source resistance vs sampling time) are in the STM32F401RE datasheet (DS10086), ADC characteristics


ADC registers
§11.12 — p. 229: ADC_SR — p. 229, ADC_CR1 — p. 230, ADC_CR2 — p. 232, ADC_SMPR2 — p. 234, ADC_SQR3 — p. 237, ADC_DR — p. 239


The analog pin mode — MODER = 11
RM0368 Rev 6, GPIOx_MODER — p. 158


HAL ADC API
UM1725 Rev 8, ADC generic driver — p. 56: HAL_ADC_Start — p. 65, HAL_ADC_PollForConversion / HAL_ADC_Start_IT — p. 66, HAL_ADC_GetValue / HAL_ADC_ConvCpltCallback — p. 68, HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel — p. 69


Sampling theory and aliasing — stated, not proven
Lee & Seshia, sensors/actuators and sampling chapters; White 2024, analog-input chapters

title: Academic References and Further Reading
text:
L11 — The Bridge to Assembly
Every listing in the deck is real output of arm-none-eabi-gcc 14.3 — the toolchain inside STM32CubeCLT — compiled for Cortex-M4 at -O0 and -O2.



Concept as taught
Where the full story is




The register file — R0–R12, SP, LR, PC, xPSR
PM0214 Rev 10, §2.1.3 Core registers — p. 18


Thumb-2 — 16- and 32-bit encodings, the .w suffix
PM0214 Rev 10, §3.1 Instruction set summary — p. 50; §3.3.8 Instruction width selection — p. 68


Memory access — LDR/STR, offsets, PUSH/POP
§3.4 — p. 69; §3.4.2 immediate offset — p. 71; §3.4.7 PUSH and POP — p. 78


Data processing — arithmetic, logic, shifts, CMP, MOV
§3.5 — p. 81: ADD/SUB — p. 83, AND/ORR/EOR/BIC — p. 85, shifts — p. 62, CMP — p. 88, MOV/MVN — p. 89


Branches and conditions — B/BL/BX, condition codes, IT
B, BL, BX, BLX — p. 142; §3.3.7 Conditional execution — p. 65; the -O2 ITE surprise: IT — p. 145


Calling convention — args in r0–r3, result in r0, LR
The Arm AAPCS32 (Procedure Call Standard for the Arm Architecture) — search “AAPCS32” at developer.arm.com; the lecture teaches only the subset visible in the debugger


Interrupt entry stacking — same stack, hardware-driven
the L06 rows above (exception model); the deck only points back to them


What the optimizer may do — folding, inlining, volatile limits
GCC manual, Optimize Options; White 2024, debugging/optimization chapters

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
section: The last question is always the same
text:
The last question is always the same

Not “does it work?” — by now it either does or it does not. The question is “can you explain it?” Point at any wire, any register, any line, and tell me why it is that way and not another.

Today you demonstrate a system, and then you answer for it individually.

Set the tone early: the defence is not an interrogation, it is the part of the assessment that only the student can do. A team cannot answer for a member.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The story so far


01 L01-L05: you learned to make one thing happen deliberately.


02 L06-L08: several things at once, without blocking.


03 L09-L11: the outside world, in and out.


04 L12: all of it together, with evidence.


05 TODAY: show it, explain it, and say what you would do differently.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Today’s objectives


01 Run a demonstration that survives contact with reality.


02 Present requirements and the evidence that each is met.


03 Defend your own contribution individually, at register level.


04 Report honestly on what did not work and why.


05 Reflect: what you would design differently now.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
What is actually assessed







Component
What it measures




Demonstration
the system meeting its stated requirements, live


Report
design decisions, evidence, and honest limitations


Presentation
can you explain the system to an engineer who has not seen it


Individual defence
what you understand, separately from your team




The first three are team marks. The fourth is not — and it is the one that most often separates two members of the same team.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The demonstration: structure
Fifteen minutes. Rehearse it; do not improvise it.


01 Setup (2 min): power up, show it running before you start talking.


02 Requirements walk (5 min): one requirement, one test, one observed result. In order.


03 Live operation (5 min): the system doing its job, including a fault you inject deliberately.


04 Known issues (3 min): what does not work, and what you know about why.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Demonstrate the failure, too

A system that only works is a demo. A system whose failure you can predict, trigger, and explain is engineering.

Inject a fault on purpose: disconnect the sensor, hold a breakpoint until ORE sets, stall the servo. Then show what the system does about it.

This is the single highest-value thing you can add to a demonstration, and almost nobody does it.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
section: When it fails on the day
text:
When it fails on the day
It happens. What distinguishes teams is the next thirty seconds.


01 Say what should have happened. You know the expected behaviour; state it.


02 Diagnose out loud. Name the species: component, resource, or timing.


03 Use your instruments. Telemetry, counters, the SFR view — they are still there.


04 Fall back. The tagged commit that worked last week. You did tag it.



A team that diagnoses a live failure convincingly can score higher than one whose demo worked and who cannot say why.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The report
Not a narrative of your term. An engineering document.


01 Requirements — testable sentences, and the result for each.


02 Design decisions — what you chose, what you rejected, and why.


03 Resource map and timing budget — from L12, updated.


04 Evidence — telemetry plots, measurements, screenshots of registers.


05 Known issues and future work — specific, not apologetic.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Design decisions are the marks
“We used TIM3 for the servo” is a fact. This is a decision:

“We put the servo on TIM3 rather than TIM2 because TIM2 was already running the LED at 1 kHz, and channels of one timer share ARR. The servo needs 50 Hz, so it needed its own timer.”


Every such sentence is a mark. Facts are free; reasons are the report.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The individual defence
Five to eight minutes each. Expect questions at three levels:


01 Your contribution: “Which parts did you write? Walk me through one.”


02 The mechanism: “Which register does that configure? What does the hardware do?”


03 The alternative: “Why this way? What would happen if you did it the other way?”



Level 3 is where marks are won. Anyone can describe what they did; explaining why the alternative is worse shows you understood the choice.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Questions you should expect


01 “Show me where you configure that peripheral. Why those values?”


02 “What is in that register right now, and why?”


03 “What would happen if I removed this line?”


04 “How do you know this works? Show me the evidence.”


05 “What is the slowest part of your system, and how do you know?”


06 “What broke during the term, and how did you find it?”



None of these can be prepared as a script. All of them can be prepared by having actually done the work.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
“I only did the software”
A common answer, and a costly one.


01 You are asked about your part in depth — but you must be able to place it in the system.


02 Which pins does your code touch? Where do they go physically?


03 What does your part cost in the timing budget?



Division of labour is fine and expected. Not knowing where your own code’s signals go is not.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Reflection: the last mark
Two questions, answered honestly:


01 What would you design differently, knowing what you know now?


02 What cost you the most time, and what would have prevented it?



“Nothing, it went well” scores nothing. Every project has an answer to both, and the specific ones are the most valuable engineering output of the term.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Common demonstration mistakes


01 UNREHEARSED: discovering the projector, the power, or the order live.


02 NO FALLBACK: the current build fails and there is nothing tagged to return to.


03 ONE PERSON KNOWS EVERYTHING: fine for the demo, expensive at the defence.


04 HIDING THE KNOWN ISSUES: they get found anyway, and cost more when they are.


05 NO EVIDENCE: claiming a requirement is met without the measurement.


06 READING THE SLIDES: you built it; talk about it.


07 CHANGING CODE THE MORNING OF: the most reliable way to break a working system.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
What good looks like

A system that meets requirements it stated in advance; evidence for each; a fault injected deliberately and explained; an honest known-issues list; and every member able to defend their own part down to the register.


Note what is not on that list: scope, polish, or novelty. A modest system, fully understood and fully evidenced, defends better than an ambitious one that half works.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Mastery checklist


✓ Run a rehearsed 15-minute demonstration with a fallback ready.


✓ State each requirement with its test and observed result.


✓ Inject a fault deliberately and explain the system’s response.


✓ Explain your own contribution at register level.


✓ Justify a design decision against its alternative.


✓ Diagnose a live failure out loud, using your own instruments.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Where this goes next


01 The method transfers. Resource maps, timing budgets, evidence-first debugging — none of that was STM32-specific.


02 The registers transfer. Every microcontroller has a timer with a prescaler, a UART with a divider, and a flag that means lost.


03 The habit transfers. “How do you know?” is the whole of engineering.



Optional extension material — DMA, displays, assembly and disassembly — is available on request if your project or your curiosity needs it.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Exit ticket
Answer for your own contribution, in writing, before you leave.


01 PART: Which parts of the system did you write, and which resources do they own?


02 MECHANISM: Name one register your code configures and say what the hardware does with it.


03 DECISION: State one design choice you made and why the alternative was worse.


04 EVIDENCE: Which requirement does your part satisfy, and how is it tested?


05 REFLECTION: What cost you the most time, and what would have prevented it?



Every concept in this course, with page-linked sources: academic references.

title: EE5203 L13 Study Sheet
text:
Demonstration, oral defence, and reflection - Basri Erdogan

Essential question: The system either works or it does not — that is settled by now. The remaining question is whether you can explain it: point at any wire, any register, any line, and say why it is that way and not another.




Run a rehearsed demonstration with a working fallback.
State each requirement with its test and the result you observed.
Inject a fault deliberately and explain the system’s response.
Explain your own contribution at register level.
Justify a design decision against the alternative you rejected.
Diagnose a live failure out loud, using your own instruments.







Component
Weight
Team / individual




Demonstration against requirements
35 %
team


Report
25 %
team


Presentation
15 %
team


Individual oral defence
25 %
individual



Two members of one team routinely receive different defence marks. That is the purpose of having one.






Time
Segment




0-2
Setup: it runs before you start explaining


2-7
Requirements walk: one requirement, one test, one result


7-12
Live operation, including a deliberately injected fault


12-15
Known issues: specific and honest



Run first, talk over it. A demo that opens with five minutes of slides has spent its best minutes on the wrong thing.



A system that only works is a demo. A system whose failure you can predict, trigger, and explain is engineering — and almost nobody does it.
Options, all rehearsable:

disconnect a sensor mid-run;
hold a breakpoint until ORE sets, then show recovery or its absence;
send an out-of-range command and show it refused;
stall an actuator and show the current draw or the reset.

State the prediction before you trigger it. Predicting correctly is worth more than the failure being graceful.




Say what should have happened. You know the expected behaviour.
Name the species — component, resource, or timing (L12).
Use your instruments — telemetry, counters, the SFR view.
Fall back to the tagged build.

Do not start editing code. A convincing live diagnosis can outscore a demo that worked but cannot be explained.










A fact (free)
A decision (a mark)




“We used TIM3 for the servo.”

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
section: Every part works. The system does not.
text:
Every part works. The system does not.

Your timer works. Your ADC works. Your UART works. You put all three in one program and the servo stutters, the display flickers, and one reading in twenty is nonsense. Nothing you tested is broken.

Integration failures are a different species from component failures, and they need a different method.

Ask for a show of hands: who has had something work alone and break when combined? This is the lecture where that stops being bad luck.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The story so far


01 L01-L05: C, registers, GPIO — one thing at a time.


02 L06-L08: interrupts and timers — several things at once.


03 L09-L11: ADC, UART, I2C/SPI — several things talking to the world.


04 TODAY: all of it, in one program, surviving a demonstration.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Today’s objectives


01 Build a resource map and find conflicts before they bite.


02 Construct a timing budget and say whether the system fits.


03 Diagnose a running system without stopping it.


04 Bisect a fault instead of guessing at it.


05 Assemble the test evidence a readiness review requires.

You have spent eleven weeks learning to find species one. Species two and three are what this lecture is about — and they are what actually breaks demonstrations.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The conflicts that actually happen


01 Same pin, two functions. PA5 is LD2 and TIM2_CH1 and SPI1_SCK. CubeMX will let you change your mind and leave the old init behind.


02 Same timer, two frequencies. Channels share ARR. The 1 kHz LED and the 50 Hz servo cannot cohabit.


03 HAL_Delay inside an interrupt. It depends on SysTick; at equal or higher priority it never returns.


04 One ADC, two channels, one rank. Reconfigured per read — so the two samples are not simultaneous.

Add up what must happen each second. Anything over 100 % is a design error, not a bug.

Now raise the LCD to 10 Hz: 72 ms per second, 7.2 % — five times the whole rest of the system. The ceiling is about 139 Hz, where the display alone consumes 100 % and nothing else ever runs.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Practice: does it fit?
A team proposes: 1 ms tick; ADC read every 10 ms; a 20-character UART line at 50 Hz; a full 16-character LCD refresh at 20 Hz; I2C at 100 kHz.


1 Compute the load of the UART and the LCD separately.


2 Does the system fit? Which item dominates?


3 Give the cheapest single change that brings it under 20 %.



UART: 20 × 10 / 115200 = 1.74 ms × 50 Hz = 8.7 %. LCD: 7.2 ms × 20 Hz = 14.4 %. Total ≈ 23 % — it fits, but the display alone costs more than everything else combined. Cheapest fix: drop the LCD to 2 Hz (1.4 %), taking the total to about 10 %.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Interrupt discipline, restated
Every rule from L06 onward, in one place:


01 A callback records; main() decides.


02 No HAL_Delay, no blocking transmit, no loops of unknown length.


03 Shared variables are volatile; multi-byte ones need care when read.


04 A callback longer than its own period is a design that cannot work.



Nearly every “random” integration failure traces back to one of these four.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
section: Debugging a system you cannot stop
text:
Debugging a system you cannot stop
A breakpoint stops the CPU. It does not stop the timer, the motor, the sensor, or the person waiting for your demo.


01 Telemetry (L10) is your instrument. Log state, not prose.


02 A GPIO pin toggled around a section costs nanoseconds and shows timing on any scope — or on an input-capture channel you already know how to use.


03 Counters for events you cannot watch: overruns, NACKs, missed deadlines. Print them once a second.



“It hangs sometimes” is not a bug report. “It hangs after 400–600 s, and ore_count is non-zero when it does” is one.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Bisection beats guessing
When a system misbehaves and you do not know why, halve it.


01 Comment out half the subsystems. Does the fault survive?


02 Yes → the fault is in the remaining half. No → it is in what you removed, or in the interaction.


03 Repeat. Six halvings isolate one line out of sixty.


04 Same method on time: git bisect between the last known-good commit and now.



Guessing scales linearly with the size of the program. Bisection scales logarithmically. That is the whole argument.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
“It worked yesterday”


01 Commit before every change you might want to undo.


02 Commit the .ioc with the generated code — regeneration is a code change.


03 Tag the version you demonstrated. You will be asked to run it again.



A team that cannot return to the version that worked last week has lost more than the code — they have lost the evidence that it ever did.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The physical layer bites last
Software-only teams meet these for the first time at integration:


01 Grounds must be common. Two supplies, no shared ground — nothing works and nothing says why.


02 Current budget. A servo stalling pulls an amp. The ST-LINK’s 3.3 V rail supplies a few hundred milliamps.


03 Brownout. The board resets mid-demo and comes back clean, so the log shows a fresh start and no error.


04 Loose jumpers. Intermittent, position-dependent, and indistinguishable from a software race.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Practice: name the species


1 The display works until the servo sweeps, then shows garbage.


2 Telemetry is perfect for ten minutes, then stops permanently.


3 The LED dims correctly but the servo never moves, from the first run.




Physical — servo current browning out the rail, or ground noise on I2C. (2) Timing/resource — very likely ORE set and never cleared. (3) Component — a plain configuration error, reproducible from the start.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
What a readiness review needs
Not “it works.” Evidence that it works:


01 A requirement list — what the system must do, in testable sentences.


02 A test for each requirement, with the result you actually observed.


03 A resource map and a timing budget that add up.


04 A known-issues list. Every real system has one; hiding it costs more marks than having it.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Writing a testable requirement







Not testable
Testable




“The display is fast”
“The display updates within 500 ms of a knob change”


“It reads temperature”
“Reported temperature is within ±2 °C of a reference between 10 and 40 °C”


“It is reliable”
“Runs 30 minutes with no reset and no lost telemetry lines”




If you cannot describe the measurement, you cannot claim the requirement — and the defence in L13 will ask you to run it.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
section: The clinic: how today’s session runs
text:
The clinic: how today’s session runs


01 Ten minutes per team. Show the system in its current state.


02 Present your resource map and timing budget — these are the checkoff.


03 Name your top three risks and what you will do about each.


04 Leave with a written list of what must be true by L13.



This is the last session before the demonstration. Bring the problem you are most afraid of, not the part you are proudest of.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Common integration mistakes


01 NO RESOURCE MAP: two owners for one timer, discovered at the demo.


02 NO TIMING BUDGET: a display refresh that cannot fit in a second.


03 BLOCKING IN A CALLBACK: everything else starves.


04 DEBUGGING BY GUESSING: changing three things at once, then not knowing which helped.


05 NO COMMITS: cannot return to the version that worked.


06 SHARED GROUND FORGOTTEN: hours lost to a wire that was never there.


07 INTEGRATING IN WEEK 14: the single most reliable way to fail this course.

Rewrite as testable requirements: “the logging is reliable” and “the motor responds quickly.”
Telemetry runs perfectly for eight minutes and then stops for good, while the LED keeps breathing. Give the most likely cause, the counter you would add to confirm it, and the fix.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Two wires, eight devices

A display, a temperature sensor, a real-time clock, an accelerometer. Four chips that have never met, sharing two wires — and every one of them knows when it is being spoken to.

Last lecture’s UART connected exactly two ends and needed no clock. Today we add a clock line, and in exchange we get addressing, acknowledgement, and a bus.

Hold up the LCD module. Point out it has four pins: power, ground, and two signal wires. Ask how a chip knows a message is meant for it.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The story so far


01 L07-L08: timers schedule work and shape signals.


02 L09: the ADC reads the analog world.


03 L10: UART carries bytes to a PC — two ends, no clock, pure agreement.


04 TODAY: synchronous buses — a clock wire, many devices, and a device that can answer back.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Today’s objectives


01 Explain what a clock line buys, and what it costs.


02 Read an I2C transaction: START, address, R/W, ACK, data, STOP.


03 Explain open-drain signalling and why pull-ups are mandatory.


04 Explain SPI’s four wires, full-duplex exchange, and the four modes.


05 Choose between I2C and SPI for a given device, with reasons.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
L10 recap: agreement without evidence
A UART transmits into the dark. If the other end is absent, misconfigured, or asleep, the sender learns nothing.


01 No clock line — both ends assume a rate.


02 No addressing — the wire goes to exactly one place.


03 No acknowledgement — nothing ever confirms receipt.



Today all three change. The clock removes the assumption, the address removes the one-to-one restriction, and the ACK removes the silence.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Adding a clock wire
In a synchronous bus, one device drives a clock line. Every bit is valid at a defined edge of that clock.


01 No baud agreement needed — the receiver is told when to look.


02 The master sets the pace, and may pause between bytes with no penalty.


03 Cost: one more wire, and one clear master.



A UART frame must be delivered at a fixed rate once started. A synchronous transfer can stop mid-byte and resume a second later — the clock simply waits.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
I2C: two wires, many devices



Wire
Name
Driven by




SCL
serial clock
the master


SDA
serial data
master and slave, at different times



Every device on the bus has a 7-bit address. All of them see every transaction; only the addressed one responds.

Two wires, up to 127 addresses, one master in this course. That is the trade I2C makes: fewer wires, more protocol.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Open drain, and why pull-ups
Both I2C lines are open drain: a device can only pull a line low. Nothing drives it high.


01 External pull-up resistors (typically 4.7 kΩ) return each line to VDD.


02 Any device may pull low at any time — so two devices talking at once cannot short each other.


03 This is what makes a shared bidirectional wire safe.



No pull-ups, no bus. The lines sit low, no START is ever seen, and every transfer times out. Most breakout boards include them — which is why forgetting them fails only sometimes.

The I2C transaction

  Master writes one byte to device 0x27

    R/W = 0
    ACK (slave)
    data bits
    …

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Addressing, and HAL’s shift
The address is 7 bits, followed by one R/W bit — together they fill one byte on the wire.


01 Datasheets quote the 7-bit address: the LCD backpack is 0x27.


02 STM32 HAL wants the 8-bit form, already shifted: 0x27 << 1 = 0x4E.


03 Pass 0x27 to HAL and you address device 0x13 — which is not there.



This single off-by-one-shift costs more lab hours than any other I2C detail. If a device will not answer, check the shift before the wiring.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
ACK: the device answers
After every byte, the receiver pulls SDA low for one clock — an acknowledge.


ACK line pulled low → “I am here, and I took that byte.”


NACK line left high → nobody at that address, or no more data wanted.



This is what a UART cannot do. HAL_I2C_Master_Transmit returning HAL_ERROR on a NACK is the bus telling you the truth: nothing answered.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
section: Practice: what is on the bus?
text:
Practice: what is on the bus?
You send address byte 0x4E, then 0x00, and the analyser shows the slave pulling SDA low after each.


1 What 7-bit address did you actually address, and was it a read or a write?


2 What do the two low pulses mean?


3 The same code with 0x27 instead of 0x4E returns HAL_ERROR. Why?



0x4E = 0100 1110: address 0x27, R/W = 0 → write. Two ACKs: the device exists and accepted both bytes. With 0x27 you address 0x13, nobody answers, NACK → HAL_ERROR.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors

Speed, and what it costs



Mode
Clock
One byte + ACK




Standard
100 kHz
90 µs


Fast
400 kHz
22.5 µs



The LCD backpack is a port expander: each character needs four I2C bytes (two nibbles, each with the enable line strobed high then low).

One character ≈ 45 bits ≈ 450 µs at 100 kHz. A full 16-character line ≈ 7.2 ms — more than seven L07 tick periods. Refresh the whole display at 10 Hz and you have spent 7 % of your CPU on a screen nobody reads that fast.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
I2C in CubeMX


01 Connectivity → I2C1: Mode I2C; PB8 = SCL, PB9 = SDA (AF4).


02 Speed 100 kHz to start — raise it only once it works.


03 The pins become open drain automatically. Check OTYPER.


04 Pull-ups: on the breakout board. Internal pull-ups are too weak for a real bus.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
SPI: four wires, one master



Wire
Name
Direction




SCK
serial clock
master → slave


MOSI
master out, slave in
master → slave


MISO
master in, slave out
slave → master


CS/NSS
chip select, active low
master → one slave



No addresses. Selection is physical: one dedicated CS line per device.

Three shared wires plus one select line per device. Two devices: five wires. Eight devices: eleven. That is SPI’s real cost, and it is the reason I2C exists.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
section: Full duplex: an exchange, not a send
text:
Full duplex: an exchange, not a send
Every SPI transfer is a swap. The master and slave shift registers are wired into one ring: for every bit clocked out on MOSI, a bit arrives on MISO.
uint8_t tx = 0xA5, rx = 0;
HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive(&hspi2, &tx, &rx, 1, 100);


01 To read, you must still write something — usually a dummy byte.


02 There is no ACK and no addressing. The wire is trusted.


03 Nothing tells you a slave is absent: reads come back 0x00 or 0xFF.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
CPOL and CPHA
Two bits decide when data is valid, and both ends must agree.


CPOL the idle level of the clock: 0 = idles low, 1 = idles high.


CPHA which clock edge samples the data: 0 = the leading edge, 1 = the trailing edge.



Get these wrong and you do not get silence — you get plausible garbage, often shifted by one bit position. That is far harder to spot than nothing at all.

Mode 0 is by far the most common. The datasheet of the slave decides; the master obeys.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Practice: read the timing diagram
A datasheet shows the clock idling high, with each data bit becoming valid on the falling edge and sampled on the rising edge.


1 What are CPOL and CPHA?


2 Which mode number is that?


3 You configure mode 0 instead. What do you observe?



Idles high → CPOL = 1. Sampled on the trailing (rising) edge → CPHA = 1. That is mode 3. With mode 0 the master samples on the wrong edge and reads each bit half a period early — consistent, shifted nonsense rather than silence.

Chip select is yours to drive
HAL_GPIO_WritePin(CS_PORT, CS_PIN, GPIO_PIN_RESET);   /* select   */
HAL_SPI_TransmitReceive(&hspi2, tx, rx, n, 100);
HAL_GPIO_WritePin(CS_PORT, CS_PIN, GPIO_PIN_SET);     /* deselect */


01 CS is an ordinary GPIO output — HAL will not toggle it for you.


02 It must stay low for the whole multi-byte transaction.


03 Releasing it between bytes resets most slaves’ internal state machines.

Many slow devices, few pins → I2C. One fast device, pins to spare → SPI. Sensors and character displays tend to I2C; SD cards, flash and pixel displays tend to SPI.

Deep dive: RM0368 Rev 6, I2C — p. 476, SPI — p. 550.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Register evidence


01 GPIOB->OTYPER bits 8 and 9 read 1 — open drain, as I2C requires.


02 A NACK sets AF in I2C1->SR1. Address a device that is not there and watch it appear.


03 SPI2->CR1 shows your CPOL/CPHA — compare against the slave’s datasheet, not against what you meant to set.


04 In loopback, SPI2->DR returns exactly what you wrote.


A successful build proves none of this. The SFR view does.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Common mistakes


01 THE 7-BIT/8-BIT SHIFT: passing 0x27 where HAL wants 0x4E.


02 NO PULL-UPS: lines stuck low, every transfer times out.


03 SDA AND SCL SWAPPED: nothing answers; a bus scan finds nothing at all.


04 IGNORING THE RETURN VALUE: HAL_ERROR on a NACK is the bus telling you the truth.


05 WRONG SPI MODE: plausible, bit-shifted garbage rather than silence.


06 CS RELEASED MID-TRANSACTION: the slave’s state machine resets between bytes.


07 EXPECTING SPI TO REPORT A MISSING SLAVE: it cannot. Reads return 0x00 or 0xFF.


08 REFRESHING THE WHOLE LCD EVERY TICK: 7.2 ms per line, spent on a display nobody reads that fast.

text:
The number nobody can see

Last lecture you acquired a real voltage and converted it to 1650. That number existed for a few microseconds inside a register, drove an LED, and vanished. Nobody watched it. Nothing recorded it.

Today the number leaves the board: onto your screen, into a log file, into a plot. And a command comes back the other way.

Open by asking how they have debugged so far: breakpoints and the Watch panel. Both stop the program. Point out that you cannot breakpoint a motor mid-flight.

The story so far


01 L06: events interrupt the program.


02 L07: a hardware counter schedules work without blocking.


03 L08: timer channels generate and measure waveforms.


04 L09: the ADC turns a voltage into a number.


05 TODAY: that number reaches a human — and a human reaches back.

02 The Watch panel shows the current value — but you cannot watch a trend.


03 Neither works on a system that must keep running: a motor, a flight, a furnace.



Debugging by stopping time only works when stopping time is allowed.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Asynchronous: no clock wire
Synchronous links (SPI, I2C — next lecture) carry a clock line: the receiver is told when to look.
A UART has no clock line. Instead both ends agree beforehand on the bit rate, and the receiver re-synchronises on every frame using the start bit.


01 The line idles high.


02 A falling edge — the start bit — says “a frame begins now.”


03 The receiver then samples at pre-agreed intervals, in the middle of each bit.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
What 8N1 means


8 data bits per frame, sent least significant first.


N no parity bit. (E = even, O = odd.)


1 one stop bit — the line returns high for at least one bit time.


So one byte costs 10 bit times: 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop. Parity would make it 11.

Both ends must agree on all four things — baud, data bits, parity, stop bits. Agreeing on three out of four produces garbage, not a warning.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
section: Practice: how long is a line?
text:
Practice: how long is a line?
Your telemetry line is raw=2048 mv=1650\r\n — 18 characters — sent at 115 200 baud.


1 How long does one line take to transmit?


2 At 10 lines per second, what fraction of the link are you using?


3 What is the fastest you could send this line, ignoring everything else?



18 × 10 / 115200 = 1.56 ms. At 10 Hz that is 1.6 % of the link. Flat out: 640 lines/s. Telemetry is cheap — until you print inside a 1 kHz loop.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Baud mismatch
The receiver samples at its bit rate, not yours. Get the rate wrong and it samples the right wire at the wrong moments.


01 Consistent garbage (same wrong characters for the same input) → baud mismatch.


02 Nothing at all → wrong port, wrong pin, or TX/RX not crossed.


03 First character wrong, rest fine → the receiver was opened mid-frame.



There is no handshake and no error message. A UART cannot tell you that you disagree — it can only hand you the disagreement.

You already have the wire
The Nucleo’s ST-LINK chip is also a USB-to-serial bridge. PA2 and PA3 are wired to it on the board.


01 PA2 = USART2_TX → ST-LINK → your PC.


02 PA3 = USART2_RX ← ST-LINK ← your PC.


03 On the PC it appears as a serial port. VS Code’s Serial Monitor opens it.



No jumpers, no USB-TTL dongle, no level shifter. The cable that flashes the board also carries your data.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
EE5203 Microprocessors
section: BRR: how the baud is made
text:
BRR: how the baud is made
USART2 sits on APB1. At the default HSI clock, PCLK1 = 16 MHz. With oversampling by 16:
\[\text{USARTDIV} = \frac{f_{\text{PCLK}}}{16 \times \text{baud}}\]
The result is stored as a fixed-point number: the top 12 bits of BRR are the integer part, the bottom 4 bits are sixteenths.
For 115 200 baud: USARTDIV = 16 000 000 / (16 × 115 200) = 8.6806 → mantissa 8, fraction 0.6806 × 16 ≈ 11 → BRR = (8 << 4) | 11 = 139 = 0x08B

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Transmitting: two flags


TXE Transmit data register empty — DR is free, you may write the next byte. The previous one may still be going out.


TC Transmission complete — the shift register is empty too. The line is genuinely idle.



TXE means “give me more.” TC means “everything has left the building.” Powering down or switching a transceiver direction needs TC, not TXE.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
HAL_UART_Transmit blocks
HAL_UART_Transmit(&huart2, (uint8_t *)buf, len, 100);
The last argument is a timeout in milliseconds. The call spins until every byte has been handed to the hardware.


01 An 18-character line at 115 200 baud blocks for 1.56 ms.


02 That is one and a half L07 tick periods, spent waiting.


03 Acceptable at 10 Hz from main(). Never acceptable inside a callback.

text:
Receiving: RXNE


RXNE Read data register not empty — a complete frame has arrived and DR holds the byte.


02 Reading DR clears RXNE — the same read-to-clear idea as the ADC’s EOC.


ORE Overrun — a new byte arrived before you read the previous one. That byte is gone.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Blocking receive is a trap
HAL_UART_Receive(&huart2, &c, 1, HAL_MAX_DELAY);   /* DO NOT */
This waits for a keystroke. Meanwhile your servo does not move, your tick does not tick, and your project appears to have crashed — because it has, from the outside.

Input arrives when a human decides, not when your loop is ready. That is exactly the situation interrupts exist for — the L06 lesson, one more source.

text:
Overrun, and why it happens
ORE sets when a byte arrives before you read the previous one. Causes, in order of likelihood:


01 Blocking somewhere long — a HAL_Delay, a slow Transmit, a breakpoint.


02 Receive interrupt never re-armed.


03 Baud far higher than the loop can drain.



HAL will not deliver further bytes until the error is cleared. Silent, permanent, and easily mistaken for a hardware fault.

The USART registers







Register

USART2->BRR
the baud divider, mantissa:fraction

One DR for both directions. Writing it loads the transmit shift register; reading it takes from the receive one. They are physically different registers behind one address.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Register evidence


01 USART2->BRR reads 0x08B for 115 200 at 16 MHz — check it against your own arithmetic.


02 GPIOA->MODER bits for PA2/PA3 read 10, and AFR[0] selects AF7.


03 Pause with a character pending: SR shows RXNE = 1; step over the read and it clears.


04 Hold a breakpoint while typing fast, then resume: ORE is set — you lost bytes and the hardware says so.


A successful build proves none of this. The SFR view does.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Common UART mistakes


01 BAUD MISMATCH: monitor at 9600, board at 115200. Consistent garbage.


02 RECEIVE NEVER RE-ARMED: exactly one byte received, then permanent silence.


03 sprintf INTO A SMALL BUFFER: silent stack corruption. Use snprintf.


04 TRANSMIT INSIDE THE CALLBACK: 1.5 ms of blocking in interrupt context.


05 ORE NEVER CLEARED: reception stops for good, looks like dead hardware.


06 \n WITHOUT \r: the monitor stair-steps instead of returning to column 1.


07 MONITOR STILL OPEN WHILE FLASHING: the port is busy and the flash fails.

TXE versus TC. TXE means “the holding register is free, give me the next byte” — the previous byte may still be shifting out. TC means the shift register is empty too and the line is idle. Powering down, or turning a half-duplex transceiver around, needs TC.



HAL_UART_Receive_IT(&huart2, &rx_byte, 1);        /* arm once */

void HAL_UART_RxCpltCallback(UART_HandleTypeDef *huart)
{
    if (huart->Instance == USART2) {
        rx_ring[head] = rx_byte;
        head = (head + 1) % RX_SIZE;
        HAL_UART_Receive_IT(&huart2, &rx_byte, 1);  /* RE-ARM - mandatory */
    }
}

The callback records; main() decides. Same discipline as every interrupt since L06.

One number from a knob

The pin was neither HIGH nor LOW. The hardware answered with a number anyway—while your program did something else.

uint16_t raw = HAL_ADC_GetValue(&hadc1);   // 2867 ?!
By the end, you will know what 2867 means, how the hardware found it in twelve guesses, and how to turn a knob, a light level, or a temperature into brightness and motion.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The story so far


01 WEEKS 4-5: pins wrote and read digital levels—high or low, nothing between.


02 WEEKS 6-7: events interrupt the program; hardware counters keep time.


03 L08: timer channels generated PWM and timestamped edges—still all digital.


04 TODAY: the last face of the pin—voltages between the levels.

Today’s objectives


01 Explain sampling, quantization, and resolution—and read the 0–4095 scale fluently.


02 Trace the SAR conversion and its timing from the 16 MHz clock.


03 Configure ADC1: channel, sampling time, single vs continuous conversion.


04 Convert counts to millivolts with integer math, and counts to control (PWM).

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
L08 recap: the channel
Thirty-second check on the timer lectures:


1 Which register turned a number into LED brightness?


2 How did we measure an unknown PWM signal?


3 What can none of that hardware tell us about a voltage?



CCR owned the duty; capture channels timestamped edges into CCR; and every input so far reported only high or low—never how much.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Beyond high and low


01 THE KNOB: a potentiometer’s position is a voltage, 0 to 3.3 V.


02 THE LIGHT: an LDR in a divider turns brightness into volts.


03 THE HEAT: thermistors—and a sensor inside the chip—speak in millivolts.


04 THE BATTERY: monitoring a supply means reading its voltage.



All of these are voltages. One peripheral reads them all: the analog-to-digital converter.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The bridge: sampling





Three verbs, every conversion: sample (freeze the voltage), quantize (pick the nearest level), encode (store the number).

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Resolution and the LSB





Our ADC has 12 bits: 4096 levels across 0–3.3 V. The staircase is finer than the noise—for us, effectively smooth.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Counts to millivolts
mV = raw × 3300 / 4095

raw =    0  →     0 mV        raw = 2048  →  1650 mV
raw = 4095  →  3300 mV        raw = 2867  →  2311 mV


01 Integer math first: (raw * 3300u) / 4095u fits comfortably in uint32_t.


02 Full scale (4095) maps to full voltage (3300 mV)—the endpoint convention.


03 Millivolts keep everything integer; convert to float only at the display edge.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Practice: read the counts


1 What raw value corresponds to 0.825 V?


2 Raw reads 3100—how many millivolts?


3 Why compute in millivolts instead of volts-as-float?



0.825 V is a quarter of full scale → ≈ 1024. 3100 × 3300 / 4095 = 2498 mV. And integers are exact, fast, and safe anywhere—including inside interrupt callbacks.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Sampling rate and aliasing





Sample slower than twice the fastest content and the samples lie—an alias. For knobs and light sensors we are safely slow; for audio and waveforms this rule bites.

In-lecture demo: aliasing, interactively.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The SAR guessing game





Binary search in silicon: one comparator decision per bit, MSB first. Our 12-bit ADC: twelve decisions per conversion.

In-lecture demo: step through a conversion.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The ADC in hardware


Simplified hardware diagram of the ADC: an analog pin feeds a sample-and-hold switch and capacitor, then the successive approximation core with comparator and internal DAC; the result lands in the data register and raises the end-of-conversion flag, which can be polled or raise an interrupt

     ADC1 — one conversion, start to finish  THE PIN PA0 · A0 analog mode    SAMPLE & HOLD switch + capacitor 3…480 cycles to charge     SAR CORE comparator vs. DAC 12 decisions, MSB first 12.5 cycles     THE RESULT ADC1->DR 0 … 4095     EOC sets in SR — ready!  poll it, or interrupt (L06 path)  Sample, decide bit by bit, publish the number. Hardware does all three. in: volts 0 – 3.3 V out: a number and a flag

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Conversion takes time







01 The ADC clock: PCLK2 16 MHz ÷ 2 = 8 MHz (divider in CCR; max 36 MHz).


02 High source impedance → the hold capacitor charges slowly → choose longer sampling. Our default: 84 cycles → ≈ 12 µs.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
One ADC, sixteen doors


01 The STM32F401RE has one ADC (ADC1) with 16 external channels—one converter, many pins.


02 PA0 is channel IN0—and the Arduino header’s A0. Our knob lives there.


03 Three internal channels need no wiring at all: a temperature sensor, V_REFINT, and V_BAT.



Channels share the one SAR core. Reading two sensors means choosing which door opens for each conversion.


Deep dive: RM0368 Rev 6, §11.3.3 Channel selection — p. 215, §11.9 Temperature sensor — p. 226.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The pin goes analog
The pin’s fourth personality, after input, output, and alternate function:


01 MODER bits = 11 — analog mode: the digital input path is disconnected entirely.


02 No pull-ups, no ReadPin, no AF—the pin wires straight to the ADC’s multiplexer.


03 The full GPIO story, complete: 00 input · 01 output · 10 alternate · 11 analog.



L04 promised the MODER table had four rows. Today the last row earns its keep.


Deep dive: RM0368 Rev 6, GPIOx_MODER — p. 158.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Single or continuous


01 SINGLE: software says go (SWSTART), the ADC converts once and stops. One question, one answer.


02 CONTINUOUS: the ADC restarts itself forever—DR always holds the freshest value.


03 SCAN: convert a whole sequence of channels in turn (with DMA—a later lecture).



We use single mode and ask on our schedule—the L07 tick decides when. Continuous returns tonight as SFR-view evidence.


Deep dive: RM0368 Rev 6, §11.3.4–11.3.5 Single / continuous conversion — p. 216.

01 Click PA0 → ADC1_IN0 (the pin turns analog—check MODER later).

The whole course in four lines—analog in, analog out:

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Common ADC mistakes


01 PIN LEFT DIGITAL: MODER not 11—you sample a pin the GPIO block still drives.


02 THE 5 V HABIT: Arduino formulas assume 5 V and 1023. Here: 3.3 V, 4095—and 5 V on an analog pin is damage, not data.


03 OFF-BY-ONE SCALE: divide by 4096 or 1023 and full scale never reads 100 %.


04 IMPEDANCE IGNORED: big resistances with 3-cycle sampling—the hold capacitor never charges; readings sag.


05 FLOAT IN THE CALLBACK: convert to millivolts with integers; pretty-print floats elsewhere.


06 POLLING BLIND: PollForConversion with no conversion started, or EOCSelection left unset—waits forever or returns stale data.

12 bits means 4096 levels, 0 … 4095. Full scale (4095) maps to full reference (3300 mV) — the endpoint convention.
Integers throughout. (raw * 3300u) / 4095u fits comfortably in uint32_t. Multiply before dividing, or you lose everything to truncation. Convert to float only at a display edge, if at all.
The reference is the ruler. Every count is relative to VREF. If the 3.3 V rail sags, every reading is wrong in the same direction, and nothing in the data shows it.

/* CubeMX: PA0 -> ADC1_IN0, PA1 -> ADC1_IN1, 12-bit,
   continuous DISABLED, EOC single conversion, 84-cycle sampling. */

uint16_t adc_read(uint32_t ch)
{
    ADC_ChannelConfTypeDef s = {0};
    s.Channel      = ch;
    s.Rank         = 1;
    s.SamplingTime = ADC_SAMPLETIME_84CYCLES;
    HAL_ADC_ConfigChannel(&hadc1, &s);

    HAL_ADC_Start(&hadc1);
    HAL_ADC_PollForConversion(&hadc1, 10);   /* waits for EOC */
    uint16_t raw = HAL_ADC_GetValue(&hadc1); /* reads DR, clears EOC */
    HAL_ADC_Stop(&hadc1);
    return raw;
}
Pace the reads from the tick, never from HAL_Delay:
if ((g_ms - t_adc) >= 10U) {            /* L07 tick schedules the read */
    t_adc = g_ms;
    uint16_t raw  = adc_read(ADC_CHANNEL_0);
    uint32_t duty = (raw * 999u) / 4095u;             /* L08's ARR */
    __HAL_TIM_SET_COMPARE(&htim2, TIM_CHANNEL_1, duty);
}
Sampling time. The input must charge the sample-and-hold capacitor through the source’s own resistance. A low-impedance source (a pot wiper) charges fast; a high-impedance one (an LDR divider, a thermistor) needs longer. Too short and the reading is dragged toward the previous channel’s value — the classic symptom of cross-talk when switching channels.
One ADC, many channels. There is one converter behind a multiplexer. To read two channels you reconfigure rank 1 and convert again — which is what adc_read(ch) does. Both readings are therefore taken at slightly different moments, not simultaneously.



MODER for PA0 reads 11 — analog. That is the fourth row of the table L04 introduced, and this is the lecture where it earns its place. In analog mode the digital input buffer is disconnected, which is both why the ADC can see the true voltage and why HAL_GPIO_ReadPin on that pin is meaningless.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
One register, two directions

This line makes LD2 glow at 25 % brightness—no loop, no delay, no interrupt. The hardware does everything.

__HAL_TIM_SET_COMPARE(&htim2, TIM_CHANNEL_1, 250);   // why 250?
Then we reverse the arrow. The same channel hardware, pointed at an input, timestamps a signal instead of making one—and the register it writes into is the one you just wrote by hand.

Live demo first if hardware is ready: change 250 to 950 and to 20, show brightness. Then promise both halves: today you generate a waveform, and then measure one back.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The story so far


01 L04-5: you set a pin high or low—two levels, nothing between.


02 L06: events interrupt the program.


03 L07: a hardware counter measures time: clock → PSC → CNT → ARR → update.


04 TODAY: that counter takes over a pin—first to generate a waveform, then to measure one.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Today’s objectives


01 Explain PWM: frequency from ARR, duty cycle from CCR.


02 Configure a PWM channel on the real 16 MHz clock; dim an LED and position a servo.


03 Reverse the channel: capture edges into CCR and recover period, frequency, and duty.


04 Choose a timer width and tick that suit the signal—and subtract timestamps wrap-safely.


05 Verify and steer a channel live from the SFR view, in both directions.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
L07 recap: the time base
Everything today sits on last week’s pipeline. Thirty-second check:


1 From 16 MHz, what do PSC = 15 and ARR = 999 produce?


2 Which register holds the live count, and what happens when it reaches ARR?


3 Why the two +1s?



1 MHz counting, update every 1 ms; CNT rolls to 0 and UIF sets; hardware divides by value + 1. If any of these felt shaky—revisit L07 before the lab.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Two levels are not enough


01 DIM AN LED: “half brightness” is not high and not low.


02 POSITION A SERVO: the motor wants a pulse width, repeated precisely.


03 DRIVE A MOTOR: speed control means controlling average power.



A digital pin has two levels—but it can switch between them fast. Control the ratio, and the average becomes any value you want.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
PWM: the duty cycle





Duty cycle = the fraction of each period spent HIGH. The LED, the motor, and your eye all respond to the average.

In-lecture demos: duty vs. mean value · PWM through an RC filter.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The mechanism: CNT vs CCR






This is the whole lecture in one figure. The sawtooth is last week’s slide — literally the same figure with one new dashed line. Spend time here.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
One new register
L07’s pipeline, plus a compare stage:


01 CNT still counts 0 → ARR, update, repeat—nothing changed.


02 Each channel adds a capture/compare register CCR1…CCR4 and a comparator against CNT.


03 In PWM mode 1 the pin is HIGH while CNT < CCR, LOW after the match.



ARR still owns the frequency. CCR owns the duty. Two registers, two independent knobs.


Deep dive: RM0368 Rev 6, §13.3.9 PWM mode — p. 336.

text:
The channel, in hardware


Simplified hardware diagram of one timer channel: the time base counter feeds a comparator against CCR1; in output-compare direction the comparator drives the PWM output logic onto pin PA5; in input-capture direction an edge detector on the same pin latches the counter value into CCR1

TIM2->CCR1     OUTPUT COMPARE PWM mode 1 logic  drives    THE PIN PA5 · LD2 alternate function AF1     INPUT CAPTURE edge detector (TI1)   listens  edge → CCR1 ← CNT  Same CCR1, two directions: compare writes the pin · capture reads the pin out: PWM today in: capture next lecture

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Frequency and duty, with numbers
For a 1 kHz, 35 % PWM from the 16 MHz clock:
16 MHz ÷ (PSC + 1)  = 16 MHz ÷ 16    = 1 MHz     (PSC = 15)
1 MHz  ÷ (ARR + 1)  = 1 MHz ÷ 1000   = 1 kHz     (ARR = 999)
duty   = CCR ÷ (ARR + 1) = 350 ÷ 1000 = 35 %     (CCR = 350)

PSC = 15 makes one tick = 1 µs. Keep it all term: every ARR and CCR is then a time in microseconds.

The pin joins the timer
The GPIO lessons return: PA5 must be handed over to TIM2.


01 MODER bits 11:10 = 10 — alternate function, the fourth mode from L04’s table.


02 AFR selects which peripheral: AF1 routes PA5 to TIM2_CH1.


03 From then on the timer drives the pin—HAL_GPIO_WritePin no longer applies.



PA5 is LD2. The LED you have blinked since L01 is wired to a timer channel—today it dims with zero wiring.


Deep dive: RM0368 Rev 6, GPIOx_AFRL — p. 162; the pin-to-AF table is in the STM32F401RE datasheet (DS10086), Alternate function mapping.

text:

01 Click PA5 → select TIM2_CH1 (replaces the GPIO_Output role it had all term).


02 In Timers → TIM2: Clock Source Internal, Channel 1 = PWM Generation CH1.


03 Parameters: Prescaler 15, Counter Period 999, Pulse 0 (start dark).


04 Generate; verify MX_TIM2_Init() and the AF pin setup in the generated GPIO code.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Start it, then steer it
HAL_TIM_PWM_Start(&htim2, TIM_CHANNEL_1);            // once

__HAL_TIM_SET_COMPARE(&htim2, TIM_CHANNEL_1, 250);   // 25 %
__HAL_TIM_SET_COMPARE(&htim2, TIM_CHANNEL_1, 800);   // 80 %


01 After Start, the hardware produces the waveform forever—the CPU is completely free.


02 Changing duty is one register write. No loop is “running the PWM.”


03 CCR is preloaded (L07’s preload lesson): the new duty takes effect at the next period—never mid-pulse, so no glitches.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Many channels, one time base


01 TIM2–TIM4 each provide four channels: CCR1 … CCR4, one comparator each.


02 All four share PSC, ARR, CNT — same frequency, independent duty cycles.


03 Four LEDs, or a servo pair, or an RGB strip—from one timer.


__HAL_TIM_SET_COMPARE(&htim3, TIM_CHANNEL_1, 250);   // 25 %
__HAL_TIM_SET_COMPARE(&htim3, TIM_CHANNEL_2, 750);   // 75 %, same 1 kHz

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Servo numbers
The 1 µs tick makes the contract trivial:
PSC = 15      → 1 MHz: one tick = 1 µs
ARR = 19999   → 20 000 µs frame = 20 ms → 50 Hz
CCR = 1000    → 1.0 ms pulse →   0°
CCR = 1500    → 1.5 ms pulse →  90°
CCR = 2000    → 2.0 ms pulse → 180°

CCR is the pulse width in microseconds. Choose units once, and the register values become readable.


Ask: what duty cycle is a 1.5 ms pulse in a 20 ms frame? (7.5 %) — then stress the servo doesn’t care about that number, only the width.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Positioning the servo
/* TIM3 CH1 on PA6 (AF2), PSC = 15, ARR = 19999 */
HAL_TIM_PWM_Start(&htim3, TIM_CHANNEL_1);

__HAL_TIM_SET_COMPARE(&htim3, TIM_CHANNEL_1, 1500);  // center: 90 deg


01 Clamp commands to 1000…2000—outside the contract, cheap servos buzz or strain.


02 The servo holds its angle as long as pulses keep coming; the timer keeps them coming.


03 Sweep by stepping CCR from the tick loop, exactly like the breathing LED.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Practice: servo at 45°


1 With the servo numbers above, what CCR commands 45°?


2 What does CCR = 2600 risk?


3 Could this servo share TIM2 with the 1 kHz LED? Why not?

01 The hardware can automate the pair: a rising edge resets CNT to zero.

01 Real edges ring and bounce—Week 6’s lesson, now on measurement inputs.

  CNT < CCR   -> output high           edge arrives -> CNT copied into CCR

/* rising edges, channel 1 direct */

/* falling edge, channel 2 indirect - high time since the last rising edge */

\[f_{\text{signal}} = \frac{1}{\text{period}} \qquad
\text{duty} = \frac{\text{high\_us}}{\text{period\_us}}\]

The cast is not decoration. On a 16-bit timer the subtraction must be done in 16 bits: captures 64000 then 1500 give (uint16_t)(1500 - 64000) = 3036, the true elapsed count. Without the cast you get a large negative number.

One update event per second

text:

01 L04: write GPIO registers directly.

text:
Today’s objectives


01 Trace the timer pipeline: clock → prescaler → counter → auto-reload → update event.


02 Calculate PSC and ARR for a required period from the real clock frequency.


03 Use a timer update event by polling and by interrupt.

EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The cost of waiting






Same LED behavior, opposite CPU budgets. Today builds the bottom row.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
section: HAL_Delay was a timer all along
text:
HAL_Delay was a timer all along

SysTick—a timer inside the Cortex-M core—has been ticking every millisecond since L01. HAL_Delay merely waits on it.



01 HAL configures SysTick at startup; its interrupt increments HAL’s own millisecond counter.


02 HAL_Delay(500) reads that counter in a blocking loop—the counting was never the problem, the waiting was.


03 Today’s tick is the same idea on a timer you control, consumed without trapping the CPU.



Deep dive: PM0214 Rev 10, §4.5 SysTick timer — p. 246.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The timer pipeline

A timer is a hardware counter that increments at a fixed rate and raises an event when it reaches a chosen value.



The timer pipeline: the 16 megahertz clock is divided by the prescaler, the counter counts the divided ticks, the auto-reload register defines the top value, and reaching it produces the update event

      TIMER CLOCK 16 MHz     PRESCALER PSC divide by PSC + 1      COUNTER CNT counts 0, 1, 2, …      AUTO-RELOAD ARR the top value      UPDATE EVENT CNT rolls to 0 flag UIF = 1 · can interrupt what the chip provides what your program consumes     

Every slide today configures or consumes one stage of this pipeline.

Walk the fragments left to right. Emphasize: the first four boxes are configuration written once; the last box is what the program lives off.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The timer clock
On our lab configuration—the default 16 MHz HSI with all bus prescalers at 1—every timer counts 16 000 000 ticks per second before prescaling.


01 The timer clock comes from the APB bus that carries the timer (TIM2 is on APB1).


02 If an APB prescaler is ever set above 1, the timer clock is twice that bus clock—check before calculating.


03 Every period calculation today starts from the real 16 MHz—not from a number found in an online example.



Deep dive: RM0368 Rev 6, §6.2 clock tree — p. 94.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The prescaler
The prescaler divides the timer clock by PSC + 1 before it reaches the counter.
counting frequency = timer clock / (PSC + 1)





PSC is 16-bit (0…65535): 15 → 1 MHz (one tick per µs) · 1599 → 10 kHz · 15999 → 1 kHz (one tick per ms). The reference manual’s name for this is the counter clock (CK_CNT).

Why not one big divider? Preview the two-knobs slide: 16-bit limits. 16,000,000 does not fit in 16 bits.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The counter
CNT increments once per prescaled tick—in hardware, in parallel with your program:


Animated plot of TIM2 CNT versus time: the counter value climbs to ARR equals 999 once per second, snaps back to zero, and the UIF flag flashes at each rollover; a marker on the vertical axis tracks the live counter value

counting frequency 1 kHz (PSC = 15999) → one update per second ARR = 999     0 500 999 TIM2->CNT 0 1 2 3 time (s)                       update event — CNT → 0, UIF = 1       update event — CNT → 0, UIF = 1  CNT climbs 0 → 999 each second 


▸ advance to run the counter



UIF is a pending bit in TIM2->SR—the same idea as the EXTI pending bit in L06.


In-lecture demo: interactive counter animation.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The auto-reload register
ARR holds the top value, so the counter visits ARR + 1 states (0 through ARR):
period = (ARR + 1) / counting frequency

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Two knobs, one period
For one update per second from 16 MHz:
16 000 000 Hz  ÷ (15999 + 1)  =  1000 Hz        (prescaler)
1000 Hz        ÷ (999 + 1)    =  1 Hz → 1 s     (auto-reload)

Split the division so both values fit in 16 bits and the intermediate frequency is a round number you can reuse—1 kHz gives millisecond resolution for free.

The opener’s two numbers are exactly these: Prescaler = 15999, Period = 999.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The +1 rule
Both divisions use the register value plus one:


01 A prescaler of 0 divides by 1—dividing by zero would be meaningless.


02 ARR = 999 means the counter visits 1000 states: 0 through 999.


03 Forgetting a +1 makes every period slightly wrong—a classic timer bug.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
The timer block, in hardware


Simplified hardware diagram of the TIM2 time base: the 16 megahertz timer clock enters the prescaler, which divides it using the PSC register; the divided clock advances the counter register CNT; a comparator matches CNT against the auto-reload register ARR, and a match produces the update event, setting UIF, reloading CNT to zero, and — if UIE is set — raising TIM2’s interrupt request to the NVIC

     TIM2 — the time base (simplified) timer clock 16 MHz (APB1)   PRESCALER ÷ (PSC + 1)  TIM2->PSC = 15999   1 kHz  COUNTER CNT ++  TIM2->CNT  runs while CR1.CEN = 1   =?  TIM2->ARR = 999  top value  match → reload CNT to 0   UPDATE EVENT UIF = 1 (SR) pending until cleared   UIE? (DIER)  TIM2_IRQn → NVIC (L06 path)

Registers you write once (PSC, ARR), one that never stops (CNT), and one bit the hardware sets for you (UIF).

The real thing: RM0368 Rev 6, Fig. 87 General-purpose timer block diagram — p. 317 — find every block from this slide in it.

text:
Practice: pick the values
Required: one update event every 200 ms from the 16 MHz timer clock.


1 Keeping the 1 kHz counting frequency, what is PSC?


2 What is ARR?


3 Give a second PSC/ARR pair that produces the same period.



PSC = 15999, ARR = 199. Alternatives abound: PSC = 1599 (10 kHz) with ARR = 1999 also gives 200 ms.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Preload and EGR
New PSC and ARR values do not necessarily act immediately:


01 PSC is always buffered: the new value is copied into use at the next update event—up to one full period later.


02 ARR is buffered only when auto-reload preload (ARPE) is enabled—the HAL default writes it immediately.


03 Writing the UG bit in TIM2->EGR forces an update event now: the buffered prescaler loads and CNT resets. This is exactly why the lab’s bare-metal init writes TIM2->EGR.



Changing a running timer’s speed? First ask when the new values take effect.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors

section: From polling to the L06 path
text:
From polling to the L06 path
Polling still spends loop time asking. The update event can instead take the exact path B1’s press took:


The timer update event follows the same interrupt path as the L06 button: the update flag raises TIM2’s interrupt request, the NVIC accepts it, the vector table selects the handler, the HAL helper clears the flag and calls the period-elapsed callback

    UPDATE EVENT UIF = 1    REQUEST TIM2_IRQn     NVIC enable · priority     VECTOR TABLE finds the handler     HANDLER + HELPER TIM2_IRQHandler() clears UIF     YOUR CALLBACK PeriodElapsed…()  L06 taught this path with EXTI13. Today only the first box changes.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Rules for the callback
L06’s rules apply unchanged:


01 Check which instance caused the interrupt.


02 Record that the event happened—set a flag, count a tick.


03 Return quickly. No HAL_Delay(), no printing, no application logic.



A 1 ms timer callback that takes 2 ms to run is a program that falls behind forever.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
EE5203 Microprocessors
EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
One tick, two schedules


One pass of the scheduler loop: check whether 500 milliseconds have elapsed and toggle the LED if so, check whether 100 milliseconds have elapsed and read the sensor if so, do other work, and repeat

   each pass   ms − t_led ≥ 500 ? no   yes  toggle LD2 · t_led = ms  ms − t_sample ≥ 100 ? no   yes  read sensor · t_sample = ms  other work  repeat







Add a third interval and the timer configuration does not change—only one more subtraction in the loop.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Practice: does it drift?
The scheduler reschedules with t_led = ms;. Suppose one loop pass occasionally takes 30 ms because of other work.


1 Can a toggle be late? By how much, at worst?


2 Does the error stay bounded, or accumulate over the next toggles?


3 What changes if the reschedule line becomes t_led += 500U;?



Both versions can be up to 30 ms late once. t_led = ms re-anchors to the late moment, so every delay pushes all later toggles—error accumulates. t_led += 500U keeps deadlines anchored: one late toggle, no long-term drift.

title: EE5203 Microprocessors
text:
Common timer mistakes


01 WRONG CLOCK ASSUMED: an online example’s 84 MHz math on our 16 MHz configuration—periods 5× too long.


02 MISSING +1: PSC = 16000 or ARR = 1000 where 15999/999 was meant.


03 CLOCK NOT ENABLED: TIM2 needs its APB1ENR bit—AHB1 was the GPIO bus.


04 NVIC FORGOTTEN: the update event fires, UIF sets, and nothing runs.


05 FLAG NOT CLEARED: polling code without CLEAR_FLAG sees an eternal event.


06 SLOW CALLBACK: work that belongs in main() running at interrupt priority.
